derivations.claim: Each $n!$ is a finite complex number, so the sequence $(n!)_{n\ge0}$ defines an element $S(g)=\sum_{n\ge0}n!g^n$ of $\mathbb C\llbracket g\rrbracket$ by [A1], irrespective of numerical convergence.

Fix any $g\ne0$ and put $t_n=n!g^n$. Then $|t_{n+1}|/|t_n|=(n+1)|g|$, which is greater than $2$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $|t_n|$ eventually grows by a factor greater than $2$ at every step, so $t_n$ does not tend to zero.

If the numerical series $\sum_nt_n$ converged, its partial sums $s_N:=\sum_{n=0}^Nt_n$ would converge, so $t_n=s_n-s_{n-1}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$; step 1.2 rules this out for every nonzero $g$. At $g=0$, the convention $g^0=1$ leaves only the constant term, so the series equals $1$. Thus the series converges at no nonzero $g$. For every $r>0$, the point $g=r/2$ lies in $|g|<r$ and gives divergence, so no positive $r$ satisfies the defining property of the radius; $r=0$ satisfies it vacuously. Therefore $R=0$ and the claimed positive radius fails.
